reviewBoundary: Six new complete senior reading passages in three practices, each consisting of one three-question text and one four-question text. Invented events and a stated thought experiment are original examples; the echo passage uses general physical explanation without invented studies or statistics. Same-author evidence/distractor review, not independent learner or teacher calibration.

units.title: 阅读理解 · 花园志愿者与风筝

materials.title: A. Become a garden welcome volunteer
materials.text:
Oak House Garden is looking for welcome volunteers for its summer opening season, from June to August. You do not need gardening knowledge. The main task is to greet visitors, explain the path choices and help them find the information they need.

Who can apply?
Applicants must be sixteen or older and able to attend at least four half-day sessions during the season. You may choose morning sessions, 9:30-12:30, or afternoon sessions, 13:30-16:30. We cannot offer accommodation or payment, but bus fares will be repaid when you show a ticket.

Training
All new volunteers must attend an in-person introduction on Saturday 24 May, 10:00-12:00. It includes a walk around the garden and practice answering common visitor questions. If you have already volunteered elsewhere, you must still attend because our routes and procedures are specific to this site.

Applying
Send a short email explaining why you would like to help and which dates you can offer. Include a contact number, but do not send identity documents at this stage. Applications close on 10 May. We will contact shortlisted applicants to arrange a brief conversation before confirming places.

Most of the role is outdoors. If standing for a whole session may be difficult, tell us in your application so we can discuss seated duties. Please do not assume you are unable to apply before talking to us.

questions.prompt: Which applicant meets the stated basic requirements?
options: An adult available for only one morning.
A fifteen-year-old available every afternoon.
A seventeen-year-old able to offer four half-day sessions.
A sixteen-year-old who requires paid accommodation.
questions.explanation: Age17 and four half-days satisfy the minimum. Fifteen is too young, one session is insufficient, and accommodation/payment are unavailable.

questions.prompt: Why must experienced volunteers attend the introduction?
options: They need to pass a gardening examination.
Only experienced volunteers may meet visitors.
The session covers this garden's own routes and procedures.
Their previous experience is assumed to be unreliable.
questions.explanation: Site-specific routes and procedures are the explicit reason. There is no gardening exam or blanket distrust of experience, and new volunteers also serve visitors.

questions.prompt: What should applicants do if prolonged standing is difficult?
options: Discuss possible seated duties in the application.
Wait until the first session before mentioning it.
Assume the role is closed to them.
Send medical identity documents immediately.
questions.explanation: The notice invites early discussion of seated duties. Documents are not requested, delaying communication is not advised, and automatic self-exclusion is discouraged.

materials.title: B. The kite's tail
materials.text:
When my cousin brought me a homemade kite, I admired its bright paper but disliked its long tail. It looked untidy beside the neat shape above it. Before our trip to the field, I untied half the cloth strips and left them on the kitchen table.

The wind was steady when we arrived. My cousin held the kite while I ran. It rose for a moment, then swung from side to side and fell. We tried three times. Each attempt ended in the grass. I blamed the wind, although other kites were flying nearby.

My cousin asked whether I had changed anything. I admitted removing the strips. She had tested this particular kite with its original tail and suggested restoring it before trying anything else. We found an old scarf in her bag and attached it carefully.

This time, the kite stayed in the air. It still moved, but its movements were smaller and easier to manage. My cousin explained that the tail was part of the design, not simply decoration. I had judged an unfamiliar object as though its appearance told me everything about its function.

Back home, I put the removed strips beside a sketch of the kite. We did not conclude that every kite needed the same tail. My cousin showed me pictures of differently shaped designs that worked in other ways. What mattered was how the parts of this one worked together.

The following weekend, we tried a smaller change, testing one arrangement at a time and keeping the original materials nearby. Some changes helped; others did not. I began enjoying the trials almost as much as watching the kite fly. The long tail still looked a little untidy to me. But now, when I wanted to improve a design, I first asked what the apparently unnecessary part might be doing.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer remove some cloth strips?
options: The writer preferred a neater appearance.
The kite could not fit through the kitchen door.
The cousin instructed the writer to shorten them.
They were too wet to carry.
questions.explanation: The writer dislikes the untidy tail beside the neat kite. Wetness, an instruction and a doorway problem are not stated.

questions.prompt: Why did the cousin suggest restoring the tail first?
options: That configuration had already been tested with this kite.
Every kite must have an identical tail.
The scarf was the only colourful object they owned.
The wind had stopped completely.
questions.explanation: She had tested this kite with its original tail. The passage later rejects universal tail requirements; steady wind and other kites contradict C, and colour ownership is irrelevant.

questions.prompt: What mistake does the writer recognise?
options: Asking the cousin about an unfamiliar object.
Treating appearance as a complete guide to function.
Trusting a test more than a photograph.
Keeping the original materials for future trials.
questions.explanation: The writer had mistaken a functional tail for decoration. A, B and D describe useful evidence, questions or preservation rather than the error.

questions.prompt: How did the later trials differ from the first change?
options: They judged success only by neatness.
They tested small changes while retaining a comparison point.
They replaced every part at once.
They assumed other kite designs were irrelevant.
questions.explanation: They change one arrangement at a time and keep original materials. A reverses the procedure; C ignores performance; D contradicts learning about different designs.

units.title: 阅读理解 · 图书馆工作间与回声

materials.title: A. Library studio rooms: booking guidance
materials.text:
The central library has two studio rooms for community groups making recordings. They are intended for spoken-word projects such as oral histories, interviews and poetry. Amplified music is not permitted because the rooms share a wall with the reading area.

Bookings are free for non-commercial projects. A group may reserve up to two hours per week, including the time needed to arrange equipment and clear the room. Groups must have at least one member aged eighteen or above who takes responsibility for the booking. Younger participants are welcome when accompanied by that member.

Before the first session, the responsible member must complete a thirty-minute equipment introduction. This is offered on Tuesday evenings and Saturday mornings. Prior experience does not remove the requirement. The library lends microphones and headphones, but users should bring a storage device for their recordings. Files left on the library computer are removed at the end of the day.

Please cancel unwanted sessions at least twenty-four hours in advance. After two missed bookings without notice, a group may lose booking access for one month. If a library equipment failure prevents your session, staff will arrange a replacement slot; it will not count as a missed booking.

The studios reduce outside noise but are not completely soundproof. We recommend a short test recording before your main work. A librarian can explain the controls, but cannot edit your finished project for you.

questions.prompt: Which project is suitable for the studio rooms?
options: A group recording with no adult member responsible.
A non-commercial interview with a local resident.
A loud band rehearsal during reading hours.
A paid advertisement requiring amplified music.
questions.explanation: A non-commercial spoken interview fits both use and fee rules. Amplified music is forbidden, and every group needs a responsible adult member.

questions.prompt: What must even an experienced first-time user do?
options: Complete the equipment introduction.
Pay for a microphone.
Leave all files on the library computer.
Book a whole day for setup.
questions.explanation: The introduction is mandatory despite experience. Equipment is lent, files should be taken away before deletion, and weekly bookings are limited to two hours including setup.

questions.prompt: What happens if library equipment failure prevents a session?
options: The group must edit its project without staff help.
It is recorded as the group's first missed booking.
The group automatically loses access for a month.
Staff arrange another slot without penalising the group.
questions.explanation: A replacement is provided and the failure does not count as a missed booking. The month's restriction concerns repeated unnotified absences, not library faults; editing help is a separate limitation.

materials.title: B. When a sound comes back
materials.text:
An echo begins with a journey. A sound reaches a listener directly, but some of its energy also travels towards a distant surface. If enough of that energy is reflected and returns after a noticeable delay, the listener may hear a repetition. The returning sound has followed a longer path than the direct one.

This description helps explain why simply entering a large room does not guarantee a clear echo. Distance matters, but so do the materials and arrangement of surfaces. Soft furnishings can absorb some sound energy. Several reflecting surfaces may return sound along different paths, producing a mixture that lasts after the original sound stops rather than one distinct repetition.

That mixture is not always undesirable. In a performance space, some reflected sound can contribute a sense of fullness. The problem is matching the room's response to its use. A sound that enriches a sustained musical note may make rapid speech harder to understand when later syllables overlap with the remains of earlier ones. A room is not acoustically good in exactly the same way for every activity.

People change the room too. An empty hall and the same hall filled with an audience need not respond alike, because bodies and clothing absorb sound differently from empty seats and bare surfaces. This is one reason a recording made during an empty-room test may not fully predict a crowded performance.

There is still value in a simple test. Clapping or speaking at different positions can reveal striking differences and suggest where to investigate. Such a test is a beginning, however, rather than a substitute for all the work needed to design a venue.

Thinking of an echo as a delayed journey shifts attention away from the voice alone. If your words return strangely, you have not necessarily spoken badly. You are hearing an interaction among the sound, the space and the position from which you listen.

questions.prompt: What makes a distinct echo possible?
options: Reflected sound returning after a noticeable delay.
The listener hearing only the shortest sound path.
All sound energy being absorbed immediately.
Every surface sending sound back at exactly the same moment.
questions.explanation: A delayed reflection can be heard as repetition. Complete absorption prevents return; the shortest path is direct sound; identical arrival from all surfaces is neither required nor stated.

questions.prompt: Why does a large room not necessarily produce one clear repetition?
options: Large rooms contain no reflecting surfaces.
Echoes depend only on the loudness of a speaker.
Materials and multiple reflection paths affect what returns.
The human voice stops producing sound indoors.
questions.explanation: Absorption and varied paths can merge reflections. A and B are false general claims, while D omits the spatial and material factors explained throughout.

questions.prompt: What does the music-and-speech comparison show?
options: Speech is improved by every increase in lingering sound.
A venue must have identical acoustic goals for all uses.
The value of reflected sound depends on the activity.
Reflections are always harmful to music.
questions.explanation: Fullness can enrich music while overlap harms rapid speech. B and C reverse or absolutise those examples; D denies the use-dependent goal.

questions.prompt: How does the author regard a simple sound test?
options: As proof that professional venue design is unnecessary.
As a way to remove every reflection instantly.
As useful only when nobody ever enters the room.
As a useful starting point with practical limits.
questions.explanation: Simple tests reveal differences and guide investigation, but do not replace venue design. The other options overstate their sufficiency, restrict their use or invent an ability to remove reflections.

units.title: 阅读理解 · 旅行投稿与画作标题

materials.title: A. Submit a journey to Along the Line
materials.text:
Along the Line is a small magazine about journeys made by public transport. We welcome personal essays that connect a specific journey with a larger question about place, work or everyday life. A list of attractions or a description that could apply to any destination is unlikely to suit us.

Send a completed essay of 800-1,200 words through our submission form. Include a brief note identifying the route and when you travelled. You do not need to be a professional writer. We accept previously unpublished work only; an essay posted publicly on your own website counts as published. Private workshop circulation does not.

Photographs are optional at the first stage. If an essay is selected, we may ask for images you own or have permission to use. Please do not send large image files with the initial submission. We will discuss a fee and any proposed editorial changes before asking you to approve publication.

We aim to reply within eight weeks. You may submit elsewhere during that period, but must tell us immediately if another publication accepts the piece. If you have heard nothing after eight weeks, a short enquiry is welcome.

We cannot provide individual feedback on every rejected submission. Rejection does not necessarily mean that the journey or essay lacks value: it may overlap with material already selected or fall outside the issue's planned focus. Read two recent issues before submitting to understand the range we publish.

questions.prompt: Which essay best fits the magazine's stated focus?
options: A complete essay linking one bus journey to changes in local working life.
A travel essay already publicly available on the writer's website.
A short proposal accompanied by a folder of large photographs.
A general list of ten famous tourist attractions.
questions.explanation: A completed specific journey linked to a larger question matches the brief. A is the rejected generic-list approach, C is already published, and D lacks the required completed essay and ignores image guidance.

questions.prompt: What should a writer do if another publication accepts the essay?
options: Wait until the magazine's eight-week period ends.
Publish both versions without telling either editor.
Inform Along the Line immediately.
Assume the submission has been automatically withdrawn.
questions.explanation: Simultaneous submission is allowed only with immediate notice of acceptance elsewhere. Waiting, assuming an automatic withdrawal and undisclosed double publication do not follow the rule.

questions.prompt: What does the notice suggest about rejection?
options: It always proves that the journey was uninteresting.
It guarantees a detailed individual explanation.
It may reflect the issue's editorial needs rather than the essay's overall worth.
It means the writer should submit the same essay every week.
questions.explanation: Overlap and issue focus can lead to rejection of valuable work. Universal lack of interest is denied; feedback is not guaranteed and repeated weekly submission is not advised.

materials.title: B. A title beside a painting
materials.text:
Imagine two labels beside the same painting. One reads 'A woman by a window'. The other reads 'Waiting for a son who never returns'. The painted marks have not changed, but the second label invites a particular story. A viewer may begin looking for grief in the woman's face rather than wondering what lies beyond the window.

This does not mean that titles control every response. A visitor may reject the suggested story or notice something the label does not mention. Nor is a neutral-sounding description entirely without influence. Naming the woman and window directs attention towards those elements, leaving other parts of the picture unnamed. The question is not whether language can be made to do nothing, but what kind of work it is being asked to do.

A title supplied by an artist and an explanation written much later can also carry different claims. An artist's title may be part of the work's intended presentation. A later account might rely on a letter, a family memory or an interpretation of the scene. If a gallery presents both in the same confident tone, viewers may find it difficult to distinguish the kinds of evidence behind them.

One response is to make that distinction available without demanding that every visitor become a specialist. A label can identify the artist's title, then mark a later interpretation as a proposal rather than a recovered certainty. A fuller account can be offered nearby for readers who want it. Briefness need not require pretending that all knowledge has the same status.

Labels remain useful. They can introduce unfamiliar subjects, connect a painting with its circumstances and open questions that a visitor might not otherwise ask. Yet a useful label should not make looking at the painting seem like checking an illustration of the label. In the thought experiment, the story about a missing son might deepen a viewer's engagement. It should also remain possible to ask whether the face actually supports that reading, and what else the image permits us to see.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the opening thought experiment?
options: To explain why paintings should never have titles.
To illustrate how wording can guide attention without altering an image.
To establish the actual identity of a painted woman.
To prove that all viewers respond identically.
questions.explanation: Different labels invite different questions while marks stay the same. No actual woman's identity is established, uniform response is later rejected, and titles are not prohibited.

questions.prompt: Why is the first label not entirely neutral?
options: It tells viewers the full story of a missing son.
It contains a known factual error about the artist.
Even simple naming highlights some elements over others.
It prevents visitors from noticing any other feature.
questions.explanation: Naming selected elements guides attention. No factual error is supplied; the missing-son story is the second label, and influence does not completely prevent other responses.

questions.prompt: What problem may arise when artist titles and later accounts use the same confident tone?
options: Visitors will be unable to read either label.
The gallery will have to remove all original titles.
Every later interpretation will become false.
Their different evidential status may be obscured.
questions.explanation: A uniform tone can conceal differences in origin and support. A invents a reading difficulty, B wrongly makes all later interpretation false, and D proposes a necessity the text does not establish.

questions.prompt: Which approach to labels does the author favour?
options: Providing helpful context while leaving interpretations open to scrutiny.
Treating all written accounts as equally certain.
Replacing the need to look closely with a definitive story.
Offering no information unless visitors are specialists.
questions.explanation: The conclusion values context and questions while retaining scrutiny of proposed readings. A subordinates the image to the label, C removes accessible guidance, and D denies the distinctions the passage recommends.
